voiceover.text: Sixteen hundred dollars for this television, and four ways to pay. Cash, if you have it all today. Lay-by, where the shop holds the TV while you pay it off, then you take it home. Buy now, pay later, from last time. Or terms, a deposit now, then a repayment every month. The repayment on terms is only seventy-eight dollars. That sounds like the easiest one to manage. These are example prices, and real offers differ, but the question is always the same. What does each way cost altogether, and which one actually suits you?

scenes.title: buying on terms: deposit plus repayments

voiceover.text: Buying on terms means paying a deposit, a first payment up front, and then the same repayment at regular times until it's paid off. You take the TV home after the deposit. Here, the deposit is twenty per cent of sixteen hundred, three hundred and twenty dollars. Then come the repayments, eighteen of them, at seventy-eight dollars each. That's fourteen hundred and four dollars. So the total cost is the deposit plus all the repayments, seventeen hundred and twenty-four dollars. Count repayments carefully. Two years of monthly repayments is twenty-four, and three years of fortnightly repayments is seventy-eight. And don't add the deposit on top of the cash price. The deposit is part of what you pay, not something extra.

scenes.title: the extra, on the cash price

voiceover.text: So how much extra does terms cost? Take the cash price away from the total. Seventeen twenty-four minus sixteen hundred is a hundred and twenty-four dollars extra. Whatever the seller calls it, the extra is built into the repayments, so the only way to see it is to add everything up. Why would anyone pay more? Because you take the TV home after paying only three hundred and twenty dollars, and the seller waits for the rest. The extra is the price of that wait. As a percentage, measure it on the cash price, the price you'd pay today. A hundred and twenty-four divided by sixteen hundred is seven point seven five per cent. Dividing by the total, seventeen twenty-four, gives about seven point two per cent, which makes the deal look better than it is.

scenes.title: every method, totalled the same way

voiceover.text: Now total all four the same way. Every dollar that leaves your hand counts. Cash is sixteen hundred. Lay-by is sixteen hundred, plus an example ten-dollar fee, sixteen hundred and ten. Buy now, pay later is eight fortnightly payments of two hundred, plus an eight-dollar account fee for each of the four months, sixteen hundred and thirty-two. Terms is seventeen twenty-four. Lay-by costs almost nothing extra, but you wait for the TV. Put them in order. Notice the smallest repayment, seventy-eight dollars, sits on the biggest total. A small repayment, repeated many times, can cost the most. So compare totals, never repayments. Terms costs ninety-two dollars more than buy now, pay later, for exactly the same TV.

But cheapest isn't automatically best. The best method depends on the buyer, so ask three questions. Can you pay cash now? Can you meet every repayment? And how urgent is it? Buyer one has seventeen hundred dollars saved. Cash is available, and it's a hundred and twenty-four dollars cheaper than terms, so cash suits her. Buyer two has two hundred dollars, and can put aside two hundred a fortnight. The old TV still works, so it isn't urgent. Lay-by suits him. He pays two hundred today and two hundred a fortnight after that, collects the TV in about three months, and pays just ten dollars extra, instead of a hundred and twenty-four on terms. And if a buyer can't meet every repayment on any plan, the honest answer is to wait and save first. A good answer names the buyer's situation, and quotes the numbers.

Here's the summary. Add every dollar that leaves your hand, then compare the totals. On terms, that's the deposit plus every repayment. A smaller repayment is not a smaller total. Then choose the method that suits the buyer.

Your turn. A fridge has a cash price of fourteen hundred dollars. On terms, it costs a ten per cent deposit, and twenty-four monthly repayments of fifty-eight dollars. Find the total cost on terms, and the extra paid as a percentage of the cash price, to one decimal place. Pause here to answer.

The deposit is a hundred and forty dollars, and the repayments are twenty-four times fifty-eight, thirteen ninety-two. So the total is fifteen hundred and thirty-two dollars. The extra is a hundred and thirty-two, and on the cash price that's nine point four per cent. Leaving out the deposit is the slip.

Last one. The same fridge can be bought with buy now, pay later. That's ten fortnightly instalments of a hundred and forty dollars, and a seven-dollar account fee for each month money is owed. The plan runs for five months. Maya's fridge has broken, and she needs a new one this week. She has five hundred dollars saved, and can put aside a hundred and forty dollars a fortnight. Find the total cost with buy now, pay later. Then justify which method best suits Maya, using your figures. Pause here to answer.

The total is fourteen hundred plus five lots of seven, fourteen hundred and thirty-five dollars. Maya can't pay cash, and she can't wait. Buy now, pay later costs ninety-seven dollars less than terms, and its hundred and forty dollar payments match what she saves each fortnight, as long as none is missed. Choosing terms just because today's deposit is smallest is the slip.

So add every dollar, then choose what suits the buyer. Now for the biggest thing most people buy before a home. Remember the red hatchback at the car yard? Fourteen thousand nine hundred and ninety dollars on the windscreen. But that's not what it costs to drive it away. What else do you pay? That's next.
